title: Adelaide Deck Replacement: When Boards, Joists or Fixings Need Attention
summary: A practical Adelaide deck replacement guide: how to distinguish surface wear from structural issues, what to inspect before requesting a quote, and how to scope a safer long-term repair.
lead: A deck can look tired for cosmetic reasons, or it can be signalling a deeper problem. Separating the two before work is priced helps homeowners make a sound decision.

sections.title: Start with the part that has actually failed
sections.summary: Raised grain, splinters, loose fasteners and localised rot can affect boards without proving that the frame has failed. Inspect joists, bearers, posts, connections and the timber where it meets the house. Soft timber, persistent movement, decay around fixings or poor drainage are reasons to investigate beyond a surface re-oil.

sections.title: Allow for Adelaide exposure
sections.summary: Sun, rain and coastal air affect decks differently. Record orientation, shade, moisture paths, proximity to the coast and whether leaf litter or planter boxes hold moisture. This gives a more useful basis for material, fixing and finishing decisions than a generic lifespan claim.

sections.title: Prepare a quote-ready scope
sections.summary: Provide wide and close-up photos, approximate dimensions, access constraints, stairs, balustrades and any built-in elements. Separate demolition, frame assessment, board replacement, handrails, finishing and waste removal so the quote is clear about fixed work and site-dependent findings.

sections.title: Choose the next step on evidence
sections.summary: A sound frame may suit selective board replacement and maintenance. Compromised load-bearing members, post bases or connections may call for a more complete repair or replacement. Discuss approvals, boundary issues and safety requirements with the relevant professional before structural changes.

title: Adelaide Custom Wardrobe Planning: How to Measure, Specify and Avoid Storage Dead Space
summary: Plan a custom wardrobe for an Adelaide home with a practical checklist for measurements, internal storage, doors, materials and installation access before final design and pricing.
lead: A wardrobe works best when its internal layout follows the way a household stores clothing, linen and everyday items—not just the dimensions of an empty wall.

sections.title: Measure the obstructions as well as the wall
sections.summary: Overall width, height and depth are only the start. Record skirtings, cornices, outlets, windows, return walls, door swings and variation in the floor or ceiling. An on-site measure before manufacture confirms cabinet dimensions, filler panels and scribe details, especially in older homes where surfaces are not perfectly square.

sections.title: Turn daily habits into internal zones
sections.summary: List what the wardrobe must store before choosing finishes. Long-hang clothing, folded garments, shoes, linen, bags and seasonal items need different clearances. A balanced layout uses adjustable shelves and dedicated hanging zones while avoiding deep, unlit shelves that become dead space.

sections.title: Select doors and materials for the room
sections.summary: Hinged doors need swing space; sliding doors preserve circulation but restrict access to one portion at a time. For wardrobes near bathrooms, laundries or external walls, discuss moisture exposure and ventilation so the substrate, edging and installation details suit the location.

sections.title: Plan the installation sequence
sections.summary: Confirm access from the street to the room, stair turns, flooring protection and the timing of paint, electrical work and carpet. Supply photos, a rough sketch, preferred finishes and the storage list when requesting a quote so the design can be measured against real use.

title: Adelaide Heritage Timber Repairs: A Practical Scope for Doors, Windows and External Joinery
summary: A practical guide to scoping heritage timber repairs in Adelaide, covering condition assessment, original details, repair-versus-replace decisions and approval checks before work begins.
lead: Heritage timber work rewards careful observation. The best first decision is often to retain and repair sound original material rather than replace it by default.

sections.title: Record what is there before proposing a solution
sections.summary: Photograph each elevation and key detail: profiles, mouldings, glazing bars, hardware, joints, paint build-up and decay. Doors and windows can have local damage at a sill, bottom rail or exposed edge while much of the original joinery remains serviceable. A condition record separates repairable fabric from components that have lost integrity.

sections.title: Make repair or replacement decisions visible
sections.summary: A good scope identifies retained timber, decayed sections to be cut back, matching timber and proposed joint locations. This makes a local splice, rebuilt sash or complete replacement comparable. Profiles matter, but water-shedding, glazing, fixing and the paint system are equally important to long-term performance.

sections.title: Check heritage and planning requirements early
sections.summary: Some Adelaide properties are subject to heritage or planning controls, particularly for external or street-facing fabric. Requirements vary by property and proposed work, so confirm current requirements with the relevant authority or a suitably qualified adviser before substantial alteration. This article is a planning guide, not legal advice.

sections.title: Give the repair a maintenance plan
sections.summary: Timber lasts longer when paint failure, failed sealant, blocked drainage and exposed end grain are addressed early. At handover, ask which parts were repaired, which finish was used, when to review it and which warning signs—cracking, sticking, water entry or soft timber—need another inspection.
